doc.title: Jamey Aebersold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 26, 2022

title: Reaction to analytical writing about solos
summary: Monk reads a magazine analysis of a solo; Aebersold doubts it helps players.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well thank you for saying that because I think mistakes or unintended notes — it may depend on who you’re working with and what age. But I can see how Michael Brecker — people might write out, transcribe Michael Brecker’s solos and point out that look he played a major third over a minor chord, and they will justify it. They will say it’s a color tone or watch because he does it seven measures later. It’s a bit of a conundrum I think. I was debating about whether to do this or not and I’m going to give it a try and get your opinion on something. This is a very small part of a lengthy analysis of a solo from a recent recording, a well known saxophone player published in a well known jazz magazine. And the scenario is it’s a tune that has many unrelated chords, one thing followed by wow where’d that come from. I’ll try to read through this fairly quickly. The idea is negotiating these unrelating chords by using common tones. So the person wrote: “His solo starts with this approach. The B flat, which is the sixth of D minor if we’re hearing Aeolian scale is the fourth of the F minor nine and the E flat seventh of the F minor is the fifth of the G sharp minor. He’s ending his lines on a note that fits both chords. It creates a forward motion effect while at the same time sounding almost modal. Then there’s a lick over the bar line at measure 45. He plays the same minor interval across the bar line — I’m almost done — but the high G flat doesn’t really fit the F minor 9. One could say that rather than resolving his line to the chord he’s letting the chord change resolve to his line. Or perhaps he’s just anticipating the chord change by half a bar.
Well that’s analysis and that’s the left side of the brain taking over. I don’t know — that sounds like something I’ve read before though, and there’s been several things in JEN J-

E-N — Jazz Education Network — that I just actually wonder about and I kind of wonder how can this be helpful to someone trying to play a blues or trying to play a tune. I don’t know. Maybe I’m still — maybe I’m still stuck back playing changes and maybe this person isn’t. I don’t know.

It seems like they go to lengths to not acknowledge that people play things they don’t necessarily mean to. And it’s like we don’t want to call them errors or mistakes, we’re just going to come up with a way that somehow justifies that particular note. And I don’t know what to say about that. Just like I didn’t know what to say about the Charlie Parker.
